Owner
OH-ner
n.
From own, Saxon agan, to possess. Webster 1828: the rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title. Scripture uses the word in case law about liability, in a prophet’s rebuke, and at the entry into Jerusalem.

Biblical Definition

Owner in Scripture appears where responsibility is being fixed. The case law of Exodus makes ownership a matter of liability rather than mere possession: If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be quit (Exodus 21:28) — and the following verse withdraws the acquittal if the owner had been warned and did not keep the animal in. God’s law distinguishes between accident and negligence, and holds a man answerable for what he owns. Isaiah opens his prophecy with the word in a rebuke that has never lost its sting: The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master’s crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider (Isaiah 1:3). Beasts recognise the man who feeds them; the covenant nation did not recognise God. Luke records the owners of a colt watching it taken: as they were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt? (Luke 19:33) — and the answer, the Lord hath need of him, was enough. And Acts 27:11 shows a centurion trusting the ship’s owner over the apostle, to the loss of the ship.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OWNER as the rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title, whether he is the possessor or not — noting that the owner and the possessor may be different persons.

expand to see more

OWNER, n. — The rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title to a thing.

Webster observes that the owner of a thing is not always the possessor, for the possessor may hold it wrongfully.

OWN, v.t. — To have the legal or rightful title to; to possess by right.

Also, to acknowledge as belonging to oneself; to avow; to confess — as, to own a fault.

From Saxon agan, to possess — the root also of own, owe, and ought.

Key Scripture

Exodus 21:28 — "If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be quit."

Isaiah 1:3 — "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider."

Luke 19:33 — "And as they were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt?"

Acts 27:11 — "Nevertheless the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul."

Modern Corruption

Scripture treats private property as real and protected while making the owner answerable to God for what he holds, which cuts against both the collectivism that denies ownership and the absolutism that treats property as beyond moral claim.

expand to see more

The eighth and tenth commandments presuppose property: there is no theft if nothing is owned, and no coveting of a neighbour’s goods if he has none. Naboth’s refusal to sell his vineyard to a king is upheld by God and Ahab’s seizure judged. Peter says to Ananias of his land, whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? — the sin was the lie, not the ownership. So the collectivist claim that property is theft has no purchase here. But the owner is not sovereign over what he owns. The earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof (Psalm 24:1); the land in Israel could not be permanently sold because the land is mine (Leviticus 25:23); gleanings belonged to the poor by law; and Exodus 21:29 makes a man liable for the harm his property does when he was warned and did nothing. Ownership under God is stewardship with title.

Isaiah 1:3 turns the word into the sharpest rebuke in the prophets, and it works by comparison with animals. An ox knows the man who feeds it; a donkey knows its master’s crib; Israel does not know its owner and does not consider. The failure is not intellectual but relational, and the chapter goes on to describe a people busy with sacrifices, new moons and appointed feasts that God says His soul hates. Religious activity had continued while recognition of God had stopped. That is a diagnosis a busy and well-attended church should read slowly, since nothing in Isaiah 1 suggests that the offerings had declined.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew baal (H1167), an owner, a lord, a husband; qanah (H7069), to acquire, to buy; Greek kurios (G2962), lord, owner; naukleros (G3490), a shipowner.

expand to see more

Hebrew baal (H1167) — an owner, master, husband; the owner of the ox shall be quit (Exodus 21:28).

Hebrew qanah (H7069) — to get, to acquire, to buy; behind the ox knoweth his owner (Isaiah 1:3).

Greek kurios (G2962) — lord, owner, master; the owners thereof said unto them (Luke 19:33), and the church’s title for Christ.

Greek naukleros (G3490) — a shipowner; the master and the owner of the ship (Acts 27:11).

Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward; the New Testament’s standing description of a believer’s relation to what he holds.

Usage

"The owner of the ox shall be quit (Exodus 21:28) — liability distinguished from accident, and fixed on the owner."

"The ox knoweth his owner… but Israel doth not know (Isaiah 1:3) — the sharpest comparison in the prophets."

"The owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt? (Luke 19:33) — and the Lord hath need of him was enough."
